title: Mannheim water capacity and development servicing agreements
subtitle: Also: street design guidelines, hybrid buses, traffic pilot, Hydrocut trail review, council security concerns and AMO nomination.
overview: Council spent most of the night on the Mannheim water capacity constraint that has paused new development servicing agreements in Kitchener, Waterloo and parts of Cambridge, Woolwich and Wilmot. It set a first release of 20 L/s to area municipalities on July 1, 2026, usable no earlier than September 30, 2026, with further quarterly releases. It also adopted a transfer framework for existing servicing commitments and directed staff to prepare administrative agreements with area municipalities. These agreements would let area municipalities sign forward-looking servicing agreements with developers. Staff will report back on July 8.

Council also approved Street Design Guidelines with a new principle recognising rural, agricultural and township contexts. It approved the purchase of 19 hybrid transit buses, a right-turn-on-red prohibition pilot at 12 intersections, and expropriations for road work on Fountain Street North and University Avenue East. It nominated Councillor Joe Gowing for the AMO board and asked staff to report on the Hydrocut stewardship agreement.

Several councillors also raised concerns about security after a disruption at the meeting. They asked staff to return with proposed next steps. After closed session, council ratified five Waterloo Regional Heritage Foundation appointments.

decisions.detail: Council assigned 20 L/s to area municipalities on July 1, 2026, available for use no earlier than September 30, 2026, with later allocations assigned quarterly from October 1, 2026 {{vote:m14}}.

Council adopted the Servicing Agreement Transfer Framework for the Mannheim Service Area, directed staff to implement it immediately, and delegated signing authority to the Commissioner of Planning, Development and Legislative Services {{vote:m18}}.
Council directed staff to prepare administrative agreements with area municipalities by July 8, 2026 to enable forward-facing servicing agreements within the allocation schedule {{vote:m21}}.

decisions.item: Forward-looking servicing agreements for draft-approved plans
decisions.detail: Council directed staff to work with area municipalities and landowners with draft plan approval before May 6, 2026 on a framework, to be reported on July 8 {{vote:m19}}.
Council approved the June 2026 Street Design Guidelines, amended to add a principle reflecting urban, rural, agricultural and township contexts {{vote:m12}}.
Council approved buying 19 hybrid transit buses from New Flyer Industries Canada to replace end-of-life buses, with delivery expected in 2027.

decisions.item: Committee recommendations on roads, airport and fares
decisions.detail: Council approved expropriations for Fountain Street North and University Avenue East, a right-turn-on-red prohibition pilot at 12 intersections, Affordable Transit Program fare updates, and the airport growth plan {{vote:m9}}.
Council directed staff to report in fall 2026 on amending the Hydrocut Stewardship Agreement and to engage the Hydrocut through the Regional Forest Management Plan {{vote:m25}}.

debate: Staff said the interim risk management framework keeps 102 L/s in reserve for unplanned outages and that a fixed 10 per cent resiliency target would not fit planned repairs. A delegate argued the reserve could be lowered because the system has a built-in buffer.

Developers and builders' representatives said approvals without water certainty make financing and sales difficult. Delegates called for faster action, a simpler process run by area municipalities, and less risk placed on developers and home buyers. A lawyer said the draft agreement language was too uncertain.

On transfers, one delegate argued water previously committed to registered plans should be usable now. Staff said that capacity no longer exists under the new methodology. Staff also said the revised wording to execute agreements immediately did not align with their policies. Council adopted the wording anyway.

On the Street Design Guidelines, councillors raised the part-gravel, part-paved shoulder design as unsafe for horse-drawn buggies. Staff said it was a compromise reached after consulting rural road users and the Mennonite community. A cycling advocacy delegate supported the guidelines and asked for more separated paths and sturdier cycling-lane separation.
Some councillors questioned waiving notice of motion for the Hydrocut item and raised concerns about late-circulated motions and limited time to review them.
